2026 · Research Note 18

Can a large machine-learning catalyst model make a prediction that survives an actual electrochemical experiment?

Open Catalyst Project adsorption-energy calculations screen bimetallic surfaces and point to PdAu3, which is then synthesized and tested for oxygen reduction.

In brief

QuestionCan a large machine-learning catalyst model make a prediction that survives an actual electrochemical experiment?
ResultRotating-disk experiments showed an improved ORR onset potential for polycrystalline PdAu3 nanoparticles compared with commercial polycrystalline Pt/C.
Why it mattersThe study explicitly connects a pretrained ML catalyst model to a targeted experimental electrocatalyst decision.
Machine-Learning-Guided Design of Pd–Au Electrocatalysts for the Oxygen Reduction Reaction
Darik A. Rosser et al. · ACS Applied Energy Materials · Published 21 August 2026
DOI: 10.1021/acsaem.6c02281

The electrochemical problem

Machine-learning catalyst models can now estimate adsorption energies over large numbers of surfaces, but a fast calculation is only scientifically valuable if it leads to a useful experimental question. Oxygen reduction provides a good test because its activity depends strongly on intermediate binding and crystal facet.

The authors focus on a structural challenge: high-index Pt facets are generally less active than Pt(111), so they ask whether a bimetallic catalyst can reduce that facet sensitivity.

What the researchers did

The team used machine-learning relaxation and adsorption-energy calculations from the Open Catalyst Project to screen bimetallic materials across crystal facets and key ORR intermediates.

The screening identified PdAu3 as a candidate expected to overcome the unfavorable structural effect. PdAu3 nanoparticles were then synthesized and evaluated electrochemically using rotating-disk linear-sweep voltammetry and Tafel analysis.

What they found

Polycrystalline PdAu3 nanoparticles showed an improved ORR onset potential compared with commercial polycrystalline Pt/C in the reported electrochemical measurements.

The important point is the direction of information flow: the pretrained ML model narrowed a large surface space to a specific bimetallic hypothesis, and that hypothesis was tested rather than left as a computational ranking.

Why this matters

Foundation-scale catalyst datasets and pretrained models are most compelling when they change laboratory decisions. This paper illustrates one route from broad adsorption-energy prediction to a focused electrocatalyst experiment.

It also shows why electrochemical domain knowledge remains necessary. The screening question is framed around known ORR scaling relationships and facet effects rather than asking a model to discover an undefined objective.

One important caution

An improved onset potential is one performance metric. It does not by itself establish superior mass activity, long-term durability, precious-metal utilization, or full-cell performance.

The experiment therefore validates the specific catalyst-design hypothesis, while broader claims about replacing Pt-based ORR catalysts would require additional electrochemical and device-level evidence.

Primary source

Darik A. Rosser et al. Machine-Learning-Guided Design of Pd–Au Electrocatalysts for the Oxygen Reduction Reaction. ACS Applied Energy Materials (2026). DOI: 10.1021/acsaem.6c02281.
